title: Achadh mhòr's wide field is cleared under Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
summary: A household near Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh clears and banks the widest single field the eastern country has yet cut from the rough, laying its bank on the stones of an older wall whose builders none of them can name, and grows in a good year wheat enough for three households where before there had been land for none.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh's boats come to be kept at Baile ghlas
summary: Boats drawn up in stone and turf sheds at Baile ghlas along the lake shore come, within a generation, to put out oftener than An Cnoc Ruadh's own strand, so that the harbour built beside the hill grows quietly into the hill's chief fishing ground.

title: Achadh naomh fences its spring before it raises a house
summary: Settlers at Achadh naomh lead a spring round in channels of their own digging and fence it before a single wall is raised, so that a stranger coming on the place first might take the water, and not the people, for what had been settled there.

title: Two households at Caol shean give their disputed landing to no one
summary: Rather than let a quarrel over a stretch of river landing run on with no keeper near enough to draw a lot on it, two households of Caol shean sit out a night together and give the ground to the landing itself, for whoever has a boat drawn up there and no other claim; the households are, within two generations, thoroughly mixed by marriage.

title: Ailis is born east of the vein
summary: A girl named Ailis is born at what will become Dùn dhearg, into a household already turf-cutting for the fort's first bank, and grows up along the ditch's edge hearing, at her own hearth, tellings of a king beyond the vein who does not grow old.

title: A trader tells Ailis of the gate at Dùn ìseal
summary: A cloth-trader passing through Caol shean's landing tells the children at a hearth of standing at the very gate of Dùn ìseal and seeing a young-faced man come in at it who has held that hill, by every account at the gate, since before its walls were built; the child Ailis asks whether it does not frighten his own children to grow old beside him, and gets no clear answer.

title: The households east of the vein raise the double bank at Dùn dhearg
summary: Owing nothing to Dùn ìseal and asking leave of no one, the households of the eastern country dig a deep ditch and raise a double bank at Dùn dhearg, sharing out the labour and afterward the ground within it by households and not by standing, so that the fort itself sets, without any law behind it, the custom the country keeps from then on.

title: A holdout household is left outside Dùn dhearg's second bank
summary: A family that refuses to send hands to the digging is simply left with its grazing outside the second bank when the ground is drawn, and asks within a generation, of its own accord and under no compulsion, to be let in on the same terms as its neighbours, its late hands reckoned at somewhat less than hands sent early.

title: Ailis's husband is buried on the slope above Dùn dhearg
summary: The net-mender of Caol shean whom Ailis married in her twenty-second year dies at Dùn dhearg an old man by any island's reckoning, and is carried out and laid on the slope above the houses with his own net-needle set in the ground at his feet.

title: Ailis sets out for the ford with seal-skins
summary: In her eighty-first year Ailis of Dùn dhearg carries three winters' store of seal-skins the length of the island toward Cruinneachadh an Àtha, meaning to trade them for salt and to stand in the river of the old tellings before her legs fail her; six of that country go with her, the first of Dùn dhearg's people to make the journey.

title: The east reaches the ford after five days on the road
summary: Ailis's party finds households along the road who have never heard of the country east of the vein, and sleeps a night with a family whose grandfather claims a telling, four hands removed, of An Cruinneachadh Mòr held in the three-thousandth year of the Grove; by the fourth day they walk unremarked among a general traffic of salt- and wool-carriers bound the same way.

title: Ìomhar Dearg names the east 'the short-lived' at the ford
summary: At the fire where Catrìona hears Ailis out, Ìomhar Dearg, holding river-grazing nearby, asks carelessly why ground should be troubled over for people who will all be dead within one of his own lifetimes, and calls them, in that breath, the short-lived; Ailis answers that she has five days' walking behind her and no wish to spend any of what time she has left arguing with a man who will have five centuries to be sorry in.

title: Young Catrìona gives Dùn dhearg ground at the ford
summary: Catrìona, of the king's blood and not yet two hundred and twenty-five years old, hears Ailis of Dùn dhearg out at the ford, asks after the double bank and whether it answers to anyone, and gives the eastern households ground of their own on the far bank, this year and every year after, asking no oath in return and receiving none.

title: Salt is carried home to Dùn dhearg without any oath given
summary: Ailis's party trades its seal-skins for salt enough to see three households through a hard winter and walks home east of the vein without having sworn anything to the ford or to the hill, and the elders of Dùn dhearg agree, hearing it told, that ground held and no word owed for the holding suits them exactly as it stands.

title: Ailis dies on the slope above the double bank
summary: Ailis dies at eighty-five in her own house on the eastern slope of Dùn dhearg's bank, three years after her one journey to the ford, and is buried beside her husband; her grandchildren keep the tale of the seal-skins and the woman of the king's blood who asked nothing back for the ground she gave.
